BBC News, 19 Oct 2026 15:02 GMT

Prime minister visits Aberfan ahead of 60th anniversary of 'horrifying tragedy'

Prime Minister Andy Burnham laying a wreath at the Aberfan cemetery. He is wearing a dark suit. The flowers are white and red.

Andy Burnham (middle) visited the Aberfan memorial garden alongside survivor Jeff Edwards (left) and Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock

Prime Minister Andy Burnham has visited Aberfan ahead of the Welsh mining village marking 60 years since a coal waste tip collapsed and engulfed a school, killing 144 children and adults.

Burnham laid a wreath at the memorial garden on Monday, alongside survivor Jeff Edwards, who was one of the last children to be brought out alive from the rubble, and Welsh Secretary Stephen Kinnock.

\"It's been 60 years since one of the most horrifying tragedies this country has ever seen. All of those children lost,\" Burnham said.

On 21 October 1966, 116 children and 28 adults were killed when a colliery spoil tip collapsed, catastrophically engulfing a primary school and surrounding houses.

A scene of devastation caused by the mining waste tip sliding down the mountainside

A survivor who spoke to the prime minister said that although she felt some \"guilt\" and missed those who died, it was important for her to talk about what happened.

The prime minister said the tragedy was something his parents had told him about when he was growing up, adding that he was there to \"recognise the community\" and what they had been through.

\"The strength of the community today is something to see and something to feel,\" he said.

\"To say also to them, I don't think Aberfan was treated properly by the authorities and that also needs to be recognised.

\"Because at a moment like this, I think all of those things need to be said and it's right that the prime minister is here to say that to them.\"

Burnham met with residents at the Aberfan Community Centre

Burnham spent about 15 minutes in the memorial garden, before speaking to people who had gathered outside, and visiting a community centre.

Burnham also addressed coal tip safety in former mining communities in south Wales.

\"It's of critical importance that we make sure that all of the remaining tips around Wales are safe indeed across the country,\" he said, adding he represented a former mining community in Makerfield near Manchester.

He said his government was providing around £140m to the Welsh government, who were \"adding some extra funding themselves\".

\"There's an organisation that is being set up to manage all of these ongoing risks,\" he said.

Irene Hollet, who survived the disaster, said it was important to talk about what happaned

Burnham met with survivors of the tragedy, including Irene Hollett, a former pupil at Pantglas school, who said it was a difficult time but that it was important for her to speak about what happened.

\"A lot of stuff comes back to you. You feel grateful that you are still around 60 years on, but then you miss your friends and family that we lost at the time,\" she said.

\"You can fell a bit of guilt that you are still here.

\"It's a difficult time, but it's got to happen. All of this has to happen for nothing ever to be forgotten\".

She said the conversation she and her fellow survivors had with the prime minister was \"pleasant\".

\"We were laughing about being naughty in school, how we played truant, and we just chatted about who we were and how we are all together today,\" she said.

Marilyn Brown lost her daughter Janette in the Aberfan disaster

Marilyn Brown's children were in Pantglas school and she lost her daughter Janette, but her son was saved by a teacher.

She said: \"I didn't realise he was saved because he'd run up from the school and I had run up to the school, and we sort of passed one another.

\"But I didn't think Janette would die. In my mind, she was still alive.

\"We stood up at the top by the school, and all the women were together, and I ran from the house.\"

Speaking to BBC, she recalled that her daughter didn't want to go to school that day, but Brown and her husband told her \"you've got to\".

She then watched her children walk up the street to school.

\"I thought, 'oh, I'll sit down now and have a cup of tea,'\" she said.

\"I sat down. It wasn't there hardly any time at all, and my nephew run down the street and said, 'you'd better come up to the school... there's something gone wrong.'\"

Brown ran up the street in her slippers and remembers being stood waiting for \"a long, long time\" to find out what was happening.

\"We didn't realise then the children had died,\" she said.

\"It's still there. It'll never go away, and I hope people will remember, and they have today.\"

Burnham has been described by survivors of Aberfan as 'very down-to-earth' and 'respectful'

Brown described Burnham as \"very nice, very down-to-earth and very, very respectful\".

While sat around a table with him, Brown said she \"didn't say about losing a child\" or that she \"was a survivor\".

\"We didn't really say an awful lot to him,\" she said, but he made them \"feel very comfortable\", which she described as \"lovely.\"

Holly told the prime minister her family had a close connection with the tragedy

Pupils from Caegarw Primary School in nearby Mountain Ash, Rhondda Cynon Taf, were on a visit to the memorial garden - built on the site of the destroyed Pantglas School, on Monday morning - unaware that the prime minister would also be there.

Burnham met pupils including Ellis, 10, whose granddad travelled across the valley to Aberfan to help with the rescue effort.
